item.title: Gate of Hell: Rise of Demons v2.0 — Art Refresh, Page Background, and the Recently Updated Badge
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Gate of Hell's first major art pass is live — a re-painted pixel-art banner, a dedicated full-page background that tiles down the play page, the new "v2.0" title across all 11 locales, and an UPDATE badge on the catalogue card. No gameplay balance changes; this is a visual relaunch. Why each change happened and what's not in this patch.
item.content:encoded:
Gate of Hell has lived in the id-1 catalogue slot since ArcadeDeck launched — the platform's pixel-art demon-survival tower defense, the original Korean-language release, and the title most likely to be the first game a new visitor clicks. It is also the game we have touched the least since it shipped. Today's update is the first real pass over its presentation: a re-painted banner, a dedicated full-page background, the "v2.0" suffix across all 11 locales, and an UPDATE badge that surfaces it on the new Recently Updated row on Home. Live now on the Gate of Hell page.

TL;DR — this is a visual update, not a balance patch

Re-painted catalogue banner. A new dedicated page background that tiles full-width down the play page. "v2.0" appended to the title in en, ko, ja, zh, de, es, es-LA, fr, pt, ru, vi. Green-cyan UPDATE badge on the catalogue card, surfaced top of the Recently Updated row on Home. Leaderboard is untouched. Existing Depth scores stand — your old runs still count toward the May-June Hall of Fame archive.

What changed

1. New banner art

The original 360w and 640w catalogue banners were early visual placeholders that did not match the in-game pixel-art tone — a colour-saturated stock-feeling render against a game that is hand-pixelled, palette-restricted, and deliberately bleak. The replacement is painted in the same palette the game itself uses: obsidian black, hellfire orange, soul-fragment magenta, arcane cyan. It runs through the same WebP optimisation the rest of the catalogue uses, so the responsive srcset behaves identically.

If you have the game card in your bookmarks bar or pinned on the Home grid, the only thing you should notice is the art. Filename, slug, route, leaderboard ID — all unchanged.

2. Dedicated page background

Gate of Hell is the first game on the platform to ship a per-game page background. Before today, every play page sat against the same global background image. The new field on the Game type — pageBg — is optional, and when set, the play page tiles that art full-width down the page instead of falling back to the global one.

The tiling shape matters. We tile vertically (repeat-y) rather than using cover or fixed. Two reasons: fixed backgrounds cause measurable CLS on mobile when the URL bar collapses on scroll, and cover stretches portrait art into pixel-soup on wide viewports. Repeat-y keeps the art at native resolution and lets it extend cleanly past long score tables and comment threads.

Other games will not all get this

Per-game backgrounds are an opt-in pattern, not a rollout. Games with abstract or low-contrast banners (most of the puzzle and idle catalogue) will keep the global background — a dedicated page background only helps when the art has strong directional pull and clear silhouettes. Expect to see it land on three or four titles this year, not eighteen.

3. Title bump to "v2.0" across all 11 locales

The English title now reads Gate of Hell: Rise of Demons v2.0. The suffix is applied in every locale — en, ko, ja, zh, de, es, es-LA, fr, pt, ru, vi — and the per-locale translations were written by the catalogue's translation owner, not auto-generated. Korean players see the suffix rendered in the locale's existing typographic convention; CJK locales get the appropriate spacing rather than a forced ASCII appendage.

This matters more than it looks. Search and feed surfaces (RSS, sitemap, JSON-LD inLanguage blocks) all pick up the updated title automatically because the i18n registry is the single source of truth. There's no scattered list of hardcoded titles to drift out of sync.

4. UPDATE badge and Recently Updated surfacing

The catalogue card now wears the green-cyan UPDATE badge — the same one introduced for the Timing Chef patch earlier in May. The badge anchors a lastUpdated timestamp (2026-05-14 in this case), which feeds the new Recently Updated row on Home. The row sorts by that timestamp descending and hides itself the moment a search query or genre filter is active, so it doesn't pollute filtered discovery.

The Recently Updated row exists for exactly this case: a launch-era title that's been on the catalogue long enough to slip out of organic discovery, but is alive enough to warrant a re-presentation. Without that surfacing, an art refresh would be invisible to anyone who already had the old card committed to muscle memory.

Why a visual-only relaunch

Three reasons, in roughly the order they mattered during planning.

The original art was a placeholder; the gameplay wasn't. Gate of Hell shipped with combat, economy, and pacing that have held up across two years of leaderboard data. The art was the weakest piece of the package and the one we kept meaning to address. Fixing it in isolation — without bundling in a balance pass — is the cheapest way to materially improve the game's presentation.

Balance changes on a leaderboard game require a score reset. Art does not. A tuning patch would have forced a Depth leaderboard wipe and reset all existing rankings to keep the board honest. Players who have spent two years pushing their Depth number deserve a heads-up before that happens. Splitting art and balance into separate updates means today's relaunch is purely additive — nothing lost, only the presentation improved.

Why we isolated the variables

If we shipped art and balance together and player feedback came back "the game feels different," we wouldn't know which change drove the perception. Holding art and balance apart means the next round of player feedback isolates the visual response cleanly — useful data when the balance pass actually lands.

A re-presented game earns one extra meaningful Home surfacing. The Recently Updated row only fires when lastUpdated moves. An art refresh is a legitimate reason to move it; an aesthetic-neutral micro-patch isn't. The threshold is deliberately editorial — we want the row to feel curated, not chronological.

Why these changes, not others

Three things we considered and explicitly did not ship in this pass.

A balance pass. Tempting because long-tail Depth scores at the top of the leaderboard have compressed — the gap between rank 1 and rank 10 is smaller than the gap between rank 10 and rank 50, which usually signals the late-game ceiling has been mapped. We held it because mixing balance changes with an art relaunch would muddle the player feedback we actually want to read. The balance pass is on the roadmap; it will get its own patch-notes post and its own leaderboard reset.

A second leaderboard track. We considered adding a secondary "Soul Fragments Spent" sort to differentiate efficient players from grindy ones at the same Depth. The dual-sort migration is a structural change to the Firestore data model and we did not want to ship it under an art-update label. If it lands, it lands alongside the balance pass.

A Korean-only locale event. Gate of Hell's language: "KO" origin makes a ko-locale featurette tempting — a Korean-language strategy stream, a localised Hall of Fame spotlight. We held it because a single-locale event would fragment the global Depth leaderboard, and the game's identity is platform-wide, not language-gated.

A short Depth-leaderboard primer for new players

The Recently Updated row is going to bring this post in front of players who have never opened Gate of Hell. If you are one of them, three habits will save you the first three failed runs.

1. Upgrade fire rate before placing a second tower

The early-wave economy is tight. A single fast-firing tower at the main chokepoint kills more demons per Soul Fragment than two slow towers spread across the map. Resist the instinct to fill the board; concentrate first, expand second.

2. Save Soul Fragments for Wave 10 Elites

Elite Demons start appearing around Wave 10. They have multiples of the HP of a standard demon and they are what end most first-attempt runs. Hold a reserve roughly equal to one Aegis-7 orbital strike at all times. Spending it on chip damage against a swarm is the most expensive way to play.

3. Hold the chokepoint — Depth is a single-front game

The map has one primary chokepoint and a couple of bypass paths that look tempting but are traps. Defending the chokepoint with three concentrated upgraded towers consistently outperforms a fortress-style spread. The leaderboard sorts by Depth alone — surviving deeper from one strong line beats surviving slightly less deep from three weak ones.

The chokepoint is the whole game. Depth is what you trade for holding it cleanly.

What's next

The balance pass is queued. No firm date — we want a few weeks of post-relaunch telemetry before touching the numbers, because the visual refresh on its own may change how players play (a better-presented game tends to attract longer sessions, which inflates Depth scores without anything else changing). If the leaderboard distribution shifts meaningfully from this update alone, the balance pass needs to react to the new baseline rather than the old one.

When the balance pass ships, it will land here as a separate patch-notes post with the full reasoning, the data behind each change, and an honest note about the leaderboard reset. The May-June Hall of Fame cycle is unaffected by today's update; the next monthly recap will mention the relaunch but Depth standings are scored on gameplay alone.

Play the new build

Live now on the Gate of Hell page. The page background you'll see scrolling under the iframe is the new art. The leaderboard at the bottom is the same one your runs have always been counted on. If the relaunch pulls you back in for a session, that is exactly the shape we built the Recently Updated row to support.

Bug reports and feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports name a specific wave ("the Elite Demon spawn rate around Wave 14 feels off because…") rather than general impressions. Browse the live Depth standings or check on your archived run on the Hall of Fame page.

Towers up. Soul Fragments banked. The gate is still holding.

item.title: Falling Dodger Launches: Neon Free-Fall, Distance + Obstacle Dual Scoring
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Falling Dodger is live — an endless neon free-fall arcade run with a dual-sort leaderboard that ranks distance first and obstacles cleared as the tiebreaker. A breakdown of the run shape, why the second sort exists, and the three habits that separate first-session players from leaderboard climbers.
item.content:encoded:
Falling Dodger is live on ArcadeDeck. It's a vertical, one-axis arcade game with a simple pitch: gravity drives, you steer, and the shaft below you is full of saw blades, laser grids, and lightning. The leaderboard sorts by Total Distance first and Total Obstacles Passed as the secondary tiebreaker — and that single design choice colours every decision a serious player will make. This post is the launch note plus the early-game habits that pull a run from "two laser grids and done" into something worth submitting.

Where to play

Launch the game from the Falling Dodger page. Keyboard A/D or ←/→ to steer; touch supports a tap-or-drag on either side of the screen. No login — enter a nickname before your first run and scores submit to the global board automatically.

What's actually shipping

The launch build is the full core run: an endless vertical shaft that scrolls faster as you descend, a single steering axis, and an escalating hazard set. Saw blades close from both walls, laser grids force last-second commits, and lightning chains arc between rails to punish hesitation. One mistake ends the run. The hazard cadence is procedural inside fixed templates — meaning two runs at the same depth feel similar in difficulty but never line up exactly.

The build is mobile-first in its layout and runs cleanly on mid-range phones. Desktop keyboard play is a parallel input, not a fallback — both inputs reach the same top of the leaderboard.

Why a dual-sort leaderboard for a fall game

A pure distance leaderboard would have been the easy call. We didn't ship it because it would have flattened the strategic shape of the game in exactly one direction: more distance = more score, full stop. Players would optimise for the centerline at high speed and the hazard variety would stop mattering.

The dual sort solves that. Distance is still primary — depth is the headline number, and the player who falls farther wins ties going up the board. But when two runs end at the same meter mark, the player who threaded more obstacles wins. The implication is concrete: the tightest gap on screen is worth pursuing even when a wider lane is technically available. The leaderboard rewards a player who reads the hazard pattern, not one who hugs a safe column.

What this means for your first submissions

Don't optimise for survival alone. A 1800m run with 42 obstacles cleared will lose ties to a 1800m run with 51 obstacles cleared. If two patterns offer the same survival probability, take the one with more hazards to thread.

Three habits that separate first-session players from leaderboard climbers

Most new players bounce around 600-900m on their first attempt, hit roughly 1400m on their fifth, and plateau there unless they internalise the patterns. Three habits consistently break the plateau.

1. Read two obstacles ahead, not one

The shaft scrolls faster than your reaction window at speed. By the time a saw blade is fully on screen, the commit to dodge it should already be in motion based on what's above it. New players track the obstacle they're about to hit; experienced players track the obstacle after the one they're dodging and pre-position. Treat the visible obstacle as the prep, not the threat. The threat is the one you can't see yet.

2. Stay centered between threats, not centered in the shaft

The instinct is to drift back to the middle of the screen between hazards. That instinct is wrong at depth. The next pattern almost always opens from one side; if you're centered, you have to traverse half the shaft to reach the gap. Stay centered between the next two threats instead — usually one-third or two-thirds across the shaft. The drift to safe positioning costs less time than the dodge from a worst-case start.

3. Commit to the narrow line when distance is close

This one only applies if you're aware of your run shape — but it's the lever that moves serious submissions. When two paths offer the same survival probability and one passes through three saw blades while the other passes through one, the three-blade line is worth more. The score difference at the same depth can be 30-50 obstacles across a long run, which on the dual-sort leaderboard is the difference between top-50 and top-10.

Quick rule of thumb

Three obstacles cleared is roughly equivalent to 25-40 meters of distance on the leaderboard, depending on where you are in the rank tier. The tighter the leaderboard is at your rank, the more the obstacle count matters.

Why this fits the platform shape

ArcadeDeck's arcade catalog already has two vertical-axis games — Skyfall and Just Jump. Falling Dodger is the third, and deliberately not a clone of either. Skyfall is timer-driven and survival-shaped; Just Jump is rhythm-shaped around a single repeating input; Falling Dodger is pattern-reading around continuous spatial commits. Three games can share a vertical screen and still feel like three different skills.

The pitch we tested internally during prototyping was a single sentence: "how long can you fall, and how cleanly?" Both halves of that question had to matter independently for the game to feel different from the rest of the platform. The dual-sort leaderboard makes both halves matter; without it, the second half would have collapsed into the first within a week of launch.

What we're watching post-launch

Two things on the immediate radar. First, the distance-to-obstacle ratio in the top-10 leaderboard slots. If everyone converges on a similar ratio, the dual sort isn't doing the strategic work we built it for and we'll widen the obstacle weighting. If the top ranks spread across a range of ratios, the design is healthy and we'll leave it alone. Second, where players bounce on first attempts. If the median first run is under 400m, the opening hazard cadence is too aggressive and we'll soften the first 200m. Patch notes for any tuning land here.

A 1800m run with 42 obstacles cleared loses ties to a 1800m run with 51. That single rule shapes the whole game.

Get on the board

The leaderboard is empty as of launch — early entries set the bar for the May-June Hall of Fame archive. If you crack the top three this week, expect a feature in the next monthly recap. Bug reports and tuning feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports name a specific depth and pattern ("the lightning chain around 1200m feels unreadable because…") rather than general impressions.

Gravity does the work. The shaft does the math. See you at depth.

item.title: Timing Chef Update: Rush Hour Tuning, New Recipes, and a Tighter Perfect Window
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Timing Chef's first major patch is live: a wider recipe roster, a recalibrated perfect window, a Rush Hour mode that no longer collapses at tier 4, and a leaderboard reset to keep the new top times honest. Full patch notes and why each change happened.
item.content:encoded:
Timing Chef has been on ArcadeDeck since launch as the platform's pure rhythm-cooking entry — one input, one timing dial, one decision per ingredient. Two months of leaderboard data, a thousand-plus completed runs, and a clear pattern in where players bounce have driven the first real tuning pass. Patch is live as of today on the play page. This post is the full notes plus the reasoning behind each change.

TL;DR

Perfect-window timing is slightly tighter on early ingredients and meaningfully more forgiving on late-game ones. Eight new recipes have landed across the existing cuisines. Rush Hour mode no longer scales into impossibility at tier 4. The Total Stars leaderboard has been reset; the Receipts secondary sort is unchanged. New runs start clean today.

What changed

1. Perfect-window recalibration

The biggest change. The original perfect window was a fixed slice across every ingredient — roughly the same arc width whether you were searing a steak or simmering broth. Telemetry showed two problems with that. First, the early-game ingredients felt punishingly tight because most new players hadn't yet learned the rhythm; the median first-session run ended inside three minutes with under fifteen stars. Second, the late-game ingredients felt too easy because experienced players had internalised the cadence and were hitting Perfect on roughly 80% of attempts past tier 3.

The patch rebalances the window per-ingredient. Early ingredients (tier 1-2) get a roughly 15% wider Perfect zone — enough that new players land their first three or four Perfects in a row and learn what the feedback looks like. Late ingredients (tier 4+) get a 10-12% narrower zone, which restores the skill ceiling the leaderboard needs. The intent is that a beginner's first session feels generous and a top-50 player's fiftieth session feels demanding.

If you were in the top ten pre-patch

Your old runs are archived but the live leaderboard is reset. The tighter late-game window means previous top scores would be inflated relative to new attempts, and we'd rather everyone climb on the same scale. Top-10 finishers from the pre-patch board get a one-time featured shout-out in the next Hall of Fame recap regardless of where they land in the reset.

2. Eight new recipes

Three new entries land in the Korean cuisine track (the game's home cuisine), three in the Western track, and two in a new Dessert track that previously only had two entries. Each new recipe introduces at least one ingredient with a unique timing signature — meaning if you've mastered the existing pool, you have new cadences to read. The Dessert additions in particular use a longer hold-then-release pattern that doesn't appear in the savoury recipes.

The full list is in-game on the Recipes tab. Two highlights:

  • Tteokbokki (Korean). Three-stage timing — first the sauce reduction, then the rice cake stir, then the final glaze. The middle stage is intentionally short; rushing the reduction wastes the rest of the dish.
  • Lava Cake (Dessert). Single long pour into the centre of a heat-sensitive window. The Perfect zone is narrow but stationary, which is the inverse of most existing recipes where the zone moves. It rewards a different kind of patience.

3. Rush Hour mode no longer collapses at tier 4

Rush Hour was the most-emailed pain point. The mode escalates order frequency every 30 seconds, and prior to this patch the tier-4 escalation effectively required hitting three Perfects per second across overlapping pans. The math just didn't work — telemetry showed only two players had ever survived past tier 4, and one of those runs was a confirmed input-macro test we removed from the leaderboard.

The patch caps Rush Hour at a more honest difficulty curve. Order frequency still escalates, but the tier-4 threshold now adds a third pan slot instead of compressing order timing further. The mode rewards multitasking instead of inhuman reaction speed. The tier-5 cap remains — Rush Hour is still meant to be the bar that separates the leaderboard, not a mode anyone can finish.

4. Heat-management feedback improvements

Two small but consistently-requested feedback changes. The heat gauge now flashes amber roughly one second before a burn instead of going straight from green to red, giving players a chance to pull the pan. And the burn penalty has been reduced from a full receipt loss to a half-receipt loss — burning a dish is still expensive enough to matter, but no longer ends a Rush Hour run on a single mistake.

5. Leaderboard reset and dual-sort confirmation

The Total Stars leaderboard is reset today. The Receipts secondary sort (more receipts wins ties on equal stars) is unchanged, so the dual-sort behaviour you may have built habits around still applies. Pre-patch standings are archived internally and the top-10 will be acknowledged in the next monthly recap, but the live board starts at zero. New runs from today count toward the May-June Hall of Fame archive.

Why these changes, not others

Three things we considered and explicitly did not ship in this patch.

An undo or rewind on the timing dial. Several players have asked for a second-chance mechanic on missed Perfects. We considered it and decided against it. The game's identity is one input, one decision, one outcome per ingredient — adding an undo would turn rhythm play into puzzle play and erase the skill expression that distinguishes the leaderboard. Forgiveness mechanics are the wrong tool for a rhythm game; the right tool is a fairer window, which is what this patch does.

A difficulty selector at run start. Tempting because it would let new players opt into a wider window. Decided against because it would split the leaderboard into incompatible tracks and reduce competitive clarity. The per-ingredient window rebalance achieves most of the same accessibility benefit without fragmenting the score pool.

An autosave checkpoint mid-Rush-Hour. The mode is meant to be a single tense run, not a savable progression. Adding a checkpoint would change the emotional shape of the mode from "can I survive" to "how long do I want to grind tonight," which is a different game.

Quick rule we used during tuning

If a proposed change would let a new player feel they were improving but would not change what the top of the leaderboard looks like, it shipped. If it would let a casual player skip a skill the leaderboard rewards, it did not.

The data behind the patch

Three numbers shaped the prioritisation, all drawn from the pre-patch live leaderboard.

  • Median first-session run length: 2 min 40 s. Too short. A rhythm game's first session should last long enough for the player to feel the cadence click into place. Three minutes does not get there. The widened early window should push this median past five minutes.
  • Rush Hour completion rate past tier 4: 0.18%. Functionally zero. A mode that effectively no one finishes is not a mode; it's a wall. The tier-4 redesign should land the realistic clear rate in the 3-5% range — still demanding, no longer impossible.
  • Top-10 Total Stars spread: ±4%. Far too tight for a long-tail rhythm leaderboard. The narrower late-game window will widen that spread and restore the strategic gap between top players, which had compressed into a near-tie.

A mode that effectively no one finishes is not a mode; it's a wall.

How to feel the patch in five minutes

If you've played Timing Chef before, the fastest way to sense the changes is one casual run plus one Rush Hour attempt. The casual run will feel slightly easier in the first minute and slightly harder in the third — that's the per-ingredient rebalance. The Rush Hour attempt should land you at tier 3 or 4 even if you previously bounced at tier 2; whether tier 5 is now reachable is the question we'd like the new leaderboard to answer.

If you've never played, start with a single non-Rush-Hour run. The new wider opening window is built specifically for the first ten minutes of play. If you're not landing Perfects on your first three ingredients, something is off and we'd like to hear about it.

What's next for Timing Chef

One concrete thing on the radar over the next month: a Daily Special mode that runs one fixed recipe with a global daily leaderboard, separate from the main Total Stars board. The intent is to give players a focused single-recipe leaderboard that resets every 24 hours — a tighter, fairer comparison than the lifetime stars total. Whether it ships depends on how the May-June leaderboard data looks after a few weeks of post-patch play. If players are still converging on the same three top-scoring recipes, the Daily Special needs to exist to diversify the chase. If the new recipes spread the focus naturally, we'll hold the feature back.

Patch notes for any further tuning land here. Bug reports and feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports name a specific recipe and ingredient ("the third stage of Tteokbokki feels mistimed because…") rather than general impressions.

Play the new build

Live now on the Timing Chef page. The leaderboard is empty as of the reset — the first players on the board this week set the bar for the May-June Hall of Fame archive. If you crack the top three, expect a featured profile in the next monthly recap.

Hot pans. Tight windows. Cook clean.

item.title: Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns — Why Card-Driven Tower Defense Hits Different
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns is live on ArcadeDeck — a card-driven, hero-based tower defense that asks a different question than a traditional TD. A look at what changes when your towers are a deck instead of a build menu, and how the genre's two shapes complement each other on the platform.
item.content:encoded:
Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns is live on ArcadeDeck. It is the platform's second tower defense title — and deliberately not a clone of the first. Where Polygon Invasion TD is a clean geometry-and-chokepoints take on the genre, Mythic Defender pulls in deck-building DNA: your towers are hero cards, your build menu is a hand, and the tactical question is not just where to place but which hero to draw next. This post walks through what that design choice changes, who each game is for, and the opening-game habits that consistently clear the early waves.

What's actually shipping

The launch build is the full core campaign. A roster of mythic heroes — Thor's storm-hammer line, the rune-bound shieldmaidens, the Whispering Wood archers — drawn from a deck rather than picked from a static menu. Wave-based progression with elite and boss enemies that punish narrow loadouts. Mana banked between rounds. Upgrades that scale better than spam-placement, and a card pool that widens as you push deeper into the campaign.

Where to play

Launch the game from the Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns page. The build is PC only — keyboard and mouse, desktop browser. We're holding the mobile port until the input model genuinely fits a touch screen rather than shipping a degraded experience.

The card-driven shift

A traditional TD gives you a build menu: every tower type is always available, gated only by gold. The decision space is mostly spatial — where do these towers go, and in what order do I afford them. Mythic Defender narrows the spatial axis (the tile grid is generous; placement is rarely punishing) and widens the composition axis (you can only place what you've drawn). The result is that two players who reach wave 6 with the same gold can have radically different boards because their hands diverged.

This is the lever that makes the game replayable in a way a standard TD usually isn't. The same map plays meaningfully differently on a second run because the draw order changes the early-game commitments. If your first three cards are tanky melee, your line forms forward and you push the chokepoint aggressively. If your first three are ranged casters, you sit back and lean on your starter tank to soak. Both work. Neither is dominant.

Mythic Defender vs. Polygon Invasion TD — pick by mood

The two TDs on ArcadeDeck answer different questions. We get the email a lot — "which one should I play?" — and the honest answer is that they are different shapes, not competing builds.

  • Polygon Invasion TD is the chokepoint-and-tower-mix shape. Read the path, place your first tower at the natural pinch, mix single-target with splash before wave 6, save resources for emergency upgrades. The skill ceiling is in reading the map. The leaderboard sorts by Peak Wave first, total Kills as a tiebreaker — depth over volume. Median session: 7-15 minutes. Launch notes here.
  • Mythic Defender: Heroes Returns is the deck-and-positioning shape. Every wave you draw, decide which heroes to commit, and which to hold back. The skill ceiling is in deck management — knowing when to spend mana on a draw versus an upgrade, and when to let a card sit because the wave you'll see in two rounds rewards it. Median session is longer; the game is built for a 25-40 minute run rather than a 7-minute drive-by.

Quick rule of thumb

Want to feel a tactical map snap into focus in seven minutes? Polygon Invasion. Want to settle in for a 30-minute run where the deck reveals itself and you build a tailored response? Mythic Defender. Most players who like one end up enjoying both for different reasons.

Opening-game habits that consistently clear the early waves

Three patterns separate first-session players (typically peaking around wave 4-6 before the line collapses) from players who reliably push past the first boss on attempt two.

1. Front-load tanks at the chokepoint, casters in the rear

The single most common new-player mistake is dropping a powerful caster early because it costs less mana than the equivalent melee draw. The caster gets overrun by wave 3 and the run is functionally over. Tanky melee heroes near the chokepoint exist to keep your damage dealers alive long enough to matter. If your first hand has no melee, hold the casters and draw — do not place a fragile damage dealer at the front of the line because you have nothing else.

2. Save mana for elites, not whole waves

Mana income across a wave is roughly steady, but the spike in damage required happens only on elite-and-boss enemies. Spending your full bar on chip damage during a swarm wave is the most expensive way to play. Hold a reserve roughly equal to one upgrade or one premium summon — when the elite shows up, that reserve is the difference between a clean kill and a leak.

The boss-wave trap

Boss enemies arrive on a predictable cadence. If you've burned all your mana into a swarm two rounds before a boss is due, you have given yourself a wave with no upgrade option and no premium draw. Watch the wave counter and pace your spend.

3. Upgrade concentration beats placement spam

It feels intuitive to fill every available tile, but in practice an upgraded tier-2 hero out-damages two unupgraded tier-1s with similar combined cost. The card economy reinforces this — drawing more cards is cheap, but upgrading what's already on the board scales the existing investment. Concentrate your firepower. The line is held by depth, not breadth.

Why we shipped a second TD at all

The straightforward answer is that the genre is broader than one shape. Polygon Invasion is excellent at what it does — fast, geometric, leaderboard-tight — and a second TD that copied its structure would have added shelf-space without adding depth. Mythic Defender exists because the deck-driven version of the genre is genuinely different to play, not because we wanted a TD count of two.

Two TDs on the same platform only make sense if they ask different questions. These do.

The other reason is data. Polygon Invasion's telemetry has been clear for weeks: players who finish a run almost universally try a second one inside the same session, but the second-day return rate is lower than we'd like for a TD. Our reading is that the run loop is tight enough that a session feels complete in one sitting — the player solved the puzzle and moved on. A longer-form, deck-driven TD with run-to-run variance covers a different retention shape: the player who comes back tomorrow because today's hand was unusual and they want to see what the next one looks like. Both shapes are valid; the catalogue should hold both.

What we're watching post-launch

Two things on the radar over the next two weeks. First, deck-balance telemetry: are players converging on one dominant hero across all loadouts, or does the draw-order variance keep the meta genuinely diverse? If everyone in the top ten is leaning on the same two heroes by wave 12, that's a tuning problem and we'll address it specifically. Second, the difficulty curve at the first boss — early playtest data suggests it's the wall most players hit, and we want to know whether it's a fair wall (the player learns from dying) or a frustrating one (the player dies for reasons they can't read from the wave).

Patch notes for any tuning land in this devlog when they ship. The game is on the global leaderboard cycle starting today, so May runs count toward the May-June Hall of Fame archive.

If you want to climb

The leaderboard is empty as of launch — early entries set the bar. If you crack the top three this week, expect a feature in the next monthly Hall of Fame recap. Bug reports and tuning feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports are wave-specific ("the second boss feels overtuned because…") rather than general impressions.

Cards in hand. Heroes at the gate. The legions are not waiting.

item.title: 40th Century: Void Survivor Lands on Steam
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Our roguelite Void Survivor is now live on Steam — a beefed-up PC build of the web version with controller support, expanded ship roster, and Engineering Bay meta-progression. Web edition stays free and live; the leaderboard cycle keeps running.
item.content:encoded:
40th Century: Void Survivor — the sci-fi action roguelite that has lived on the ArcadeDeck web catalogue since launch — is now available on Steam. The PC build is a parallel release, not a replacement: the web edition stays free, stays current, and stays on the global leaderboard cycle. Steam exists for players who want a beefier package, controller-first input, and a long-term home for the game outside a browser tab.

Storefront: store.steampowered.com/app/4531420

Same game, two homes

Both editions share the core run loop, ship roster, and module pool. Web edition is the fastest way in — one click, no install, leaderboard live. Steam edition is the long session, controller-friendly, content-heavier version for the players who already log multi-hour sessions.

What's actually on Steam

The Steam build is the same engine and the same design pillars, with the additions that didn't fit a browser tab cleanly. Highlights from the launch build:

  • 7 unique ships — distinct base stats, signature modules, and tactical identity. Glass-cannon interceptors through fortress-class dreadnoughts. The web edition currently ships with a tighter roster; the rest land on web in subsequent patches as we tune them under web constraints.
  • 20+ combat modules — plasma mines, frost mirrors, chrono cannons, phantom aegis. Mix, match, and trigger Evolutions — endgame transformations unlocked by specific module pairings.
  • 4-branch passive tree — Overload, Shield, Signal, Abyss. The Heart of the Abyss capstone sits at the bottom of the tree as the long-game target.
  • Permanent Engineering Bay — run-to-run progression. Components forged from each death feed into the next pilot. This is the meta-progression layer the recent design post framed as the 10-20% rule in practice.
  • Curse & Blessing system — trade safety for power, stack risk for legendary rewards. The most-tested addition in the closed playtest, and the system that pulled top-tier runs out of the convergent loadout problem.
  • Boss gauntlet — wave kings, mini-bosses, mediums, and the Big Boss encounters that punctuate the run.
  • Tactical Artifacts — active abilities triggered mid-fight. Decoders, accelerators, stabilizers. A separate axis from passive modules.
  • Module Library & Antique Archive — every module wielded and every fallen civilization's lore is catalogued across runs. Soft progression for completionists.

Why a Steam release at all

The web edition was built for the seven-minute attention budget — a point covered in the roguelike design post and lived out in the leaderboard data. That's the right shape for the median web visitor. It is not the right shape for the player who wants a controller in hand, a 90-minute session, and the option to chase the deepest meta-progression layers without a tab fighting them for memory.

The Steam build is the long-form companion. The web build is the quick-strike one. Most players will only ever touch one of the two; that's fine. The minority who play both get a different experience from each, not a duplicate.

Web leaderboard stays separate

Steam scores do not flow into the ArcadeDeck global leaderboard, and Steam achievements are a Steam-only system. The web leaderboard remains the place where the monthly Hall of Fame cycle is decided. If you only play Steam, your runs do not count toward the Hall of Fame — that's a deliberate boundary, not a bug.

What this means for the web edition

Three concrete things, in order of how soon you'll feel them.

1. The web build is not abandoned

Patch cadence on the web edition stays the same. The Steam launch is additive — the engine, art, and balance work feed both editions, and most balance changes ship to web first because the web telemetry is denser and the iteration loop is shorter. If a tuning change is too aggressive for web, we walk it back on web specifically rather than dragging Steam through a hotfix cycle.

2. Some Steam content will land on web later

Specifically: additional ships from the 7-ship Steam roster, the full Curse & Blessing depth, and a subset of the larger module pool. Each web addition is gated on whether the system fits a sub-30-minute browser run cleanly. If a Steam-side feature would compress the median web run into a content-skipping sprint, we don't port it. The web edition's tuning constraint is real and we won't break it for parity.

3. Cross-promotion stays light-touch

The Steam page is now linked from the web game's detail page and from this post. There will not be a popup, an overlay, or a forced upsell. If you only ever play the web edition, your experience does not change. The Steam release exists for the players who already wanted it.

Under the hood

For the engineering-curious: the Steam build is shipped via Electron with the same PixiJS rendering layer and Matter.js physics core that drive the web edition. The shared engine means a balance pass on a module behaves identically across both builds — no "Steam version is 5% stronger" drift. Where the editions diverge is in input handling (full controller mapping is Steam-only at launch), asset depth (Steam ships higher-resolution variants where bandwidth was the web blocker), and meta-progression scope (Engineering Bay and Curse depth are scaled larger on Steam).

A balance pass on a module behaves identically across both builds — no "Steam version is 5% stronger" drift.

If you want to support the launch

The most useful actions, in rough order:

  1. Wishlist on Steam. Wishlists drive the storefront's algorithmic visibility more than any other signal during a launch window. Even if you don't intend to buy, a wishlist genuinely helps the page surface to the right players.
  2. Play the web edition if you haven't yet — it's free and the fastest way to sense whether the run loop fits you. The web build is at arcadedeck.net/play/40th-century-void-survivor.
  3. Tell us what feels off. Specific feedback ("the third boss feels overtuned because…") goes a long way. Mail to help@arcadedeck.net; tag the email subject with [STEAM] or [WEB] so it routes faster.

What's next

Two things on the immediate roadmap. First, a web-side patch in mid-May widens the artifact pool — the change flagged in the roguelike design post — and lands a small Curse & Blessing subset on the web edition. Second, a Steam-side patch will follow with quality-of-life work surfaced by the launch playtest: keybind remapping polish, a Steam Cloud save fix, and a balance pass on the two ships that telemetry showed converging on a single dominant build.

Patch notes for both ship to this devlog when they go live.

See you in the void.

item.title: Designing Roguelikes for the Browser: Run Length, Death, and Meta-Progression
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Roguelikes live or die on three tuning decisions: how long a run lasts, what death actually costs, and how much you let the player carry forward between attempts. A breakdown of how Dicefall Chronicles, 40th Century: Void Survivor, and Kingdom's Last Stand each answered them.
item.content:encoded:
Roguelikes are the trickiest genre we ship at ArcadeDeck. The pitch sounds simple — procedural runs, permadeath, every attempt is fresh — but the genre's history is littered with games that nailed the first run and collapsed by the tenth. The difference between a roguelike that holds players for a hundred runs and one they bounce off after three is rarely the art or the variety; it is three tuning decisions made before any content gets built. This post walks through those three decisions using our own catalogue: Dicefall Chronicles, 40th Century: Void Survivor, and Kingdom's Last Stand.

Decision one: how long is a run, really?

The most-cited number for browser roguelikes is "twenty minutes per run." It is repeated everywhere because it sounds right, and because the genre's most-played PC titles converged on similar lengths. The number is misleading. The right metric is not the length of a winning run; it is the length of an average run, including the early failures. If a player's first ten attempts each end inside three minutes because they have not learned the systems yet, the game effectively trains the player to expect short, cheap sessions. When they finally earn a 25-minute run, the late game lands as a pleasant surprise rather than a slog.

Dicefall Chronicles enforces this curve deliberately. Early-floor failures resolve in 90 seconds; mid-floor runs settle around 8-12 minutes; only deep runs into the lower dungeon stretch past 20. The progression of run lengths matches the progression of skill, which means the time investment grows with the player's confidence rather than dropping it on them in run one.

Why short failures matter

A roguelike where the first failure costs you 25 minutes is a roguelike with a brutal new-player funnel. Cheap early deaths let players experiment with risky builds without feeling punished — and experimentation is exactly what teaches the systems faster than any tutorial.

40th Century: Void Survivor takes the opposite approach: every run is roughly the same length because the wave timer is fixed. The variance is not in duration but in how deep into the artifact pool you reach before the ceiling catches you. Both shapes work, but they imply different player behaviours. Dicefall rewards patience; Void Survivor rewards intensity. The wrong call would have been to copy one shape into the other game; the right call is to pick a shape that matches the run's emotional arc.

Decision two: what does death actually cost?

Pure permadeath — the original Rogue model — costs everything. Modern roguelikes almost universally soften this, but the softening is where most designs go wrong. Two failure modes show up consistently:

  • Too soft. Death costs nothing, every run carries forward all upgrades, and the genre dissolves into a slow grind. Players stop reading the procedural content because the unlock economy is the real game.
  • Too hard. Death costs everything, including knowledge — players who lose a 40-minute run learn nothing they can apply differently next time, because the next run starts at the same baseline with different RNG. Frustration compounds.

The sweet spot is what we call a knowledge tax: death costs the run's progress but not the lessons learned. In Kingdom's Last Stand this shape is explicit. You lose your army on a wipe; you keep the elemental matchup notes and the formation patterns you discovered. The next run starts at zero gold but with a smarter player at the keyboard. The death economy works when the second run is meaningfully better than the first, even with no carried items.

Decision three: meta-progression — how much, and what kind?

Meta-progression is the most-debated lever in modern roguelike design. Two extremes:

No meta. Every run starts identical. Pure skill expression. Beloved by genre purists and a small minority of players. The retention numbers, in our experience, are unforgiving — most browser players bounce after their first three losses if there is no off-ramp.

Heavy meta. Every run permanently unlocks something — characters, items, starting bonuses. Retention soars in the first week; in the second week, players realise the unlocks are the actual progression and the procedural runs are a delivery mechanism for them. The genre's appeal — that every run is a fresh strategic puzzle — quietly evaporates.

Our internal rule is roughly 10-20% of total run impact comes from meta-progression, never more. Dicefall Chronicles unlocks new starter dice between runs, but the dice rolls themselves and the order they appear remain the heart of the game. Void Survivor's artifact pool is permanent but the pool is large enough that even after 50 runs you are still seeing combinations you have not built before. Meta-progression should make the player feel like they are getting better at the game, not getting more powerful in the game.

The meta-progression trap

If the leaderboard's top players have all unlocked the same final-tier upgrade and pure new players cannot compete, the meta is too heavy. We watch for this signal directly: top-ten leaderboard entries should be earnable within the first 5-10 hours of play, not the first 50.

What this looks like in practice

Dicefall Chronicles ran a balance pass in March that cut starting-deck size by one die. The intent was to make early runs feel less generous and force riskier dice purchases earlier. The result was that median run length dropped from 11 minutes to 8 minutes, but new-player retention into a third session jumped roughly 18%. Shorter early runs, faster failure cycles, more attempts per session — exactly the loop the genre needs to keep working.

40th Century: Void Survivor is in the opposite tuning state. Top players have started clearing the standard mode reliably, which means the run length has compressed in a different way: the late game is no longer the question, the artifact mix is. The next pass, scheduled for May, will widen the artifact pool rather than buff enemies — adding decision space rather than damage. The change matches the genre rule: when the existing decisions stop being interesting, add more decisions, not more difficulty.

Kingdom's Last Stand is the youngest of the three and is still finding its balance. Early data suggests the elemental-matchup system is doing the right work for new players (the second run is meaningfully better than the first), but the late game converges on a small number of dominant formations. We are watching specifically for whether top-ten leaderboard entries are using the same loadout. If they are, we have a meta problem and will rebalance the relevant elements before adding new content.

Meta-progression should make the player feel like they are getting better at the game, not getting more powerful in the game.

The browser constraint, explicit

Everything above is true for any roguelike. The browser context tightens the screws further. Our players show up with seven minutes of attention; some have a tab full of work waiting. A roguelike that demands a 40-minute commitment for any meaningful progress has already lost the median session. We tune for the player who has time for one or two runs in a sitting and budgets accordingly. If a build cannot pay off inside two attempts, it does not ship.

Try the games

If you want to feel these decisions firsthand, three runs each will tell you more than this post does. Start at Dicefall Chronicles for the dice-deck shape, 40th Century: Void Survivor for the fixed-length intensity, and Kingdom's Last Stand for the formation-driven version. Each has a global leaderboard; tuning notes for any of the three land in this devlog when they ship.

If you have a roguelike-specific design question we have not covered, write in to help@arcadedeck.net. The most useful prompts are concrete ("why does Dicefall feel harsher than Void Survivor on a first run?") rather than general — those are the ones we can answer with the actual numbers.

item.title: Galaxy Launch: Designing an Idle Game That Doesn't Collapse Into Grind
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Most idle games degenerate into a cookie-clicker grind by hour two. Here's how Galaxy Launch's progression curve, prestige loop, and offline cap were tuned to keep every session feeling like a decision.
item.content:encoded:
When we sketched Galaxy Launch in late 2025, the central design question was uncomfortable: can an idle game stay interesting after the first hour without resorting to flashier numbers? Most browser idle titles answer this by inflating exponents — by hour three you are clicking a button to multiply a number by another number, and the gameplay loop has dissolved into a screen-saver. We wanted Galaxy Launch to feel like a sequence of small decisions all the way through, even at idle. This post walks through the three tuning choices that shaped the launch build, with a short note on how the leaderboard data is informing what we change next.

The progression problem in one paragraph

Idle games trade short-term clicks for long-term automation. The trap is that as automation scales, the player's role shrinks. Once every upgrade pays for itself in seconds, the only meaningful interaction left is choosing when to prestige — and prestige loops, badly tuned, become the entire game by hour two. The rest of the systems become decoration. Galaxy Launch had to keep at least three live systems competing for attention at every stage of a run, otherwise it would degenerate into the same loop.

Choice 1: A capped offline yield

The most common idle-game lever is offline progress. Most titles cap it at 8-24 hours and award the full rate. We deliberately capped Galaxy Launch's offline yield at 4 hours of tier-current production, with the rate scaling down after the first hour. The result: closing the tab for a full work day no longer guarantees a meaningful jump on return.

Why a short cap helps

A long offline cap turns the game into a notification check. A short cap turns it into a session. The leaderboard data backs this up: median session length on Galaxy Launch is 7 minutes, with a long tail at 25-40 minutes. We see almost no one-minute drive-by sessions, which is exactly the engagement shape an idle game should have.

The tradeoff is real — players who want a true "set and forget" experience bounce off Galaxy Launch in their first day. We accept that. The game is built for short, intentional sessions, not for passive accumulation. The offline cap is the single biggest mechanic enforcing that shape.

Choice 2: Prestige tied to milestone reads, not gold totals

Standard idle prestige unlocks at a flat currency threshold. The pacing problem is that the threshold either feels trivial (you prestige six times in your first session and the loop loses meaning) or feels punishing (you grind for 90 minutes for a single prestige and the loop demoralises). Galaxy Launch's prestige unlocks instead at milestone reads — discrete in-game events like "first dwarf star explored" or "engine tier 4 unlocked" — each of which requires juggling at least two production tracks.

The result is that prestige timing varies by playstyle. A player who pushes a single track hard hits the milestone faster but earns a smaller prestige multiplier; a player who balances tracks earns more per prestige but takes longer to qualify. Both strategies appear at the top of the leaderboard. That diversity at the top of a ranking is the clearest signal that a system is well-tuned. If everyone in the top ten has converged on the same loadout, the design has failed.

Choice 3: A two-track currency that resists hoarding

Single-currency idle games encourage hoarding. The optimal play is almost always "save until the next big upgrade is affordable, then spend everything." That collapses decision-making into a wait. Galaxy Launch uses a two-track currency where one resource decays slowly if unspent — not enough to punish absence, but enough that holding a full bank for ten minutes costs you 5-10% of it.

Watch the decay rate

We have rebalanced the decay rate twice since beta. Too aggressive and players feel punished for thinking; too gentle and the system is invisible. The current rate (roughly 1% per minute on the secondary track only) sits in a sweet spot where high-leaderboard players notice it and casual players do not.

The decay is visible only on the secondary track, so the primary economy still feels stable. Top-five players spend the secondary continuously and treat it as a pacing tool; mid-table players forget about it and lose roughly 10-15% of their potential rate over a long run. The skill ceiling lives almost entirely in this one mechanic.

What the leaderboard is telling us

Two months post-launch, three patterns stand out. First, the gap between the top-ten and top-fifty players is mostly about prestige timing, not session count — players who prestige slightly later on average dominate. Second, no one in the top ten has spent more than 20 cumulative hours on the game, which suggests the systems are deep enough to reward focus but not so demanding that they reward grind. Third, the secondary-currency decay is doing exactly the work it was designed to do: top players' spending rate is roughly 3x the median.

No one in the top ten has spent more than 20 cumulative hours on the game.

The next tuning pass, scheduled for early May, will tighten one prestige milestone that data shows is being skipped by almost everyone (a sign it is mispriced) and add a third optional production track for late-game players. Both changes will get a patch note here when they ship.

Try it yourself

Galaxy Launch is live on the play page. The leaderboard resets monthly as part of the Hall of Fame cycle. If a specific design choice frustrates or surprises you, write in to help@arcadedeck.net — the best feedback we receive is specific ("the prestige multiplier feels off after the third reset because…") rather than general impressions.

See you in orbit.

item.title: Polygon Invasion TD: Launch Notes & Opening Strategy
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Polygon Invasion TD is live — a fast-paced tower defense built around chokepoint reads and tower-mix decisions. Launch notes plus an opening-wave plan that consistently clears the first ten waves.
item.content:encoded:
Polygon Invasion TD is the newest title on ArcadeDeck and the platform's first dedicated tower defense entry. The Polygon Dimension has breached our reality; geometric invaders march in endless formation; you build, upgrade, and hold the line. The leaderboard sorts by Peak Wave first and total Kills as the secondary tiebreaker — meaning a player who pushes deeper but kills less still beats a grindier run. That single design choice colours every decision below.

What's in the launch build

The launch ships with the full core loop: strategic tower placement, multiple tower types with upgrade paths, and an endless wave structure that scales indefinitely. Boss waves break the rhythm with high-HP single targets that punish splash-only setups, and swarm waves do the inverse — punish single-target-only setups with sheer numbers. Mouse and touch controls are both first-class, and the build runs cleanly on mid-range mobile.

Where to play

Launch the game from the Polygon Invasion TD page. Scores submit to the global leaderboard automatically — no login required, just enter a nickname before your first run.

Why TD fits the ArcadeDeck format

Most browser TDs are either too short to feel meaningful or too long to fit a casual session. We tuned wave pacing so that the first ten waves take 4-6 minutes — enough to learn the map, commit to a tower mix, and see whether your read was right. If you misplay the early game, you feel it by wave 8 and can restart without losing 30 minutes. If you play well, the run scales up cleanly past wave 20 and the leaderboard becomes a question of how far you can push before a single mistake compounds.

Opening strategy: the first ten waves

Three habits separate first-session players (typically peaking around wave 5-7) from players who reliably clear wave 10 on their second or third attempt.

1. Read the chokepoint before you place anything

The map has one or two natural chokepoints depending on enemy path. Don't drop your first tower until you've identified them. A first tower placed at the chokepoint kills more enemies than two towers placed mid-path. The early-game economy is tight — a single misplaced tower in wave 1 is the difference between affording an upgrade by wave 4 or scraping through to wave 6 under-levelled.

2. Mix tower types early, not late

The most common new-player mistake is going all-in on one tower type because it felt strong on wave 2. Single-target towers melt tanks and starve on swarms; splash towers shred swarms and stall on tanks. If you reach wave 6 with a pure single-target setup, the next swarm wave will leak. Commit to at least one of each type by wave 4, even if it means delaying an upgrade.

Boss wave reminder

Boss waves typically land on multiples of 5. If you're approaching wave 5, 10, or 15 with a splash-heavy mix and no anti-tank, sell a low-tier splash tower and replace it with a single-target before the wave starts. The refund covers most of the swap cost.

3. Save resources for emergency upgrades

Don't spend down to zero between waves. Keep a reserve roughly equal to the cost of a mid-tier upgrade. When a boss wave starts and you realise your damage is short, that reserve is the difference between a clutch upgrade mid-wave and a leaked life. The leaderboard rewards Peak Wave above all else — surviving wave 12 by one HP is worth more than dying cleanly on wave 11 with a full bank.

What we're watching post-launch

Two things on our radar over the next two weeks. First, wave-progression telemetry: where do players consistently die, and is the curve smooth or does one specific wave act as a wall? If we see a spike at, say, wave 14, we'll rebalance that wave specifically rather than flatten the whole curve. Second, tower-mix data: are players converging on one optimal mix, or is there genuine strategic variety? If everyone runs the same loadout by wave 10, that's a tuning problem and we'll address it in a patch note here.

Surviving wave 12 by one HP is worth more than dying cleanly on wave 11 with a full bank.

Get on the board

The leaderboard is empty as of launch — early entries will set the bar for the April-May Hall of Fame cycle. If you crack the top three this week, expect a feature in the next monthly recap. Bug reports and tuning feedback go to help@arcadedeck.net; the most useful reports are wave-specific ("wave 13 felt unfair because…") rather than general impressions.

See you on the leaderboard.

item.title: Triangle Battle: Running a Four-Player Couch Tournament
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: Triangle Battle's local 4-player mode is the most-requested party format on ArcadeDeck. A short guide to running a fair tournament without arguments.
item.content:encoded:
Triangle Battle was built as a couch-multiplayer first experiment: four players, one keyboard, one screen, no logins. Since launch it has consistently been our highest replay-rate game on weekends, and the most common email we get is "how do you run a fair tournament?" Here's the format we use internally and have seen work cleanly at small parties.

Hardware warning

Membrane keyboards typically support only 2-3 simultaneous key presses. In a 4-player local game this guarantees lost inputs and arguments. Use a keyboard with full N-key rollover.

Hardware

You need a USB or Bluetooth keyboard with full N-key rollover. Membrane keyboards typically support only 2-3 simultaneous key presses, which becomes a problem in a four-player game where everyone is mashing direction keys at once. If your keyboard ghosts, players will lose inputs and accuse each other of cheating. A cheap mechanical board solves this for under $40.

Bracket structure

For 4 players, run a round-robin: every player faces every other player once in 1v1 mode, then a final 4-player free-for-all. With six 1v1s plus one final, total runtime is ~25 minutes for typical match lengths. Award 3 points for a 1v1 win, 5 points for the FFA winner, 3/2/1 for second/third/fourth in the FFA. Highest total wins.

For 5-8 players, split into two pools of 3-4, run round-robin within each pool, then take the top two from each into a four-player FFA final. Keeps total runtime under 40 minutes.

Map and rule selection

Triangle Battle has three arena layouts and four hazard settings. For tournament play, we recommend:

  • Arena: Symmetric Wedge. The other two layouts have spawn-point asymmetries that cumulate over a long set. Wedge is the only fully mirrored map.
  • Hazards: Off for the round-robin, On for the FFA. Hazards spice up the final without polluting head-to-head results with random deaths.
  • Best of one per matchup. Best-of-three drags total runtime past 45 minutes and tournament fatigue starts costing players inputs.

Common arguments and how to pre-empt them

"They got the better starting position." Coin-flip starting positions before each round. We use a physical coin because it ends arguments faster than a digital one.

"My key didn't register." The N-key rollover keyboard solves this almost entirely. If a key truly didn't register and you can demonstrate it by replaying the input, replay the round. Use this rule sparingly or it gets abused.

"Final FFA isn't fair to the leader." The 5/3/2/1 weighting means the round-robin leader is favoured but not guaranteed. We've kept the format because the tension is the point — close finishes happen most when the late game can still flip the standings.

Submit your tournament

If you run a Triangle Battle tournament with 6+ players, send results plus a short write-up to help@arcadedeck.net. We feature the most interesting brackets in the monthly Hall of Fame recap.

item.title: Mastering GEM MERGE: Five Move-Saving Patterns
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: GEM MERGE rewards low move counts on its dual-sort leaderboard. Five patterns that separate top-50 finishes from top-five finishes.
item.content:encoded:
GEM MERGE looks deceptively simple — drop a gem, match three, watch them merge. The leaderboard tells a different story: ranks one through ten are separated by a handful of moves, not points. Because the secondary sort rewards lower move counts, every shuffle matters.

Here are the five patterns we see consistently in top-five replays. Each one is a cheap habit to practise; together they shave 30-60 moves off a typical full-board clear.

1. Reserve the corners

Corner cells only have two neighbours, so any gem you place there can only contribute to two potential merges. Keep corners empty until the late game and use them as overflow slots for low-tier gems you don't yet want to commit to a chain.

2. Read the queue, not the board

Beginners place each new gem next to the matching colour they can see. Top players pre-plan two to three placements ahead by reading the queue. If you see a tier-2 red incoming after the current tier-1 blue, dropping the blue away from the red prep zone is almost always the right call.

3. Build chains diagonally

Triangular merge layouts cascade better than linear ones. A diagonal stack lets a single high-tier merge resolve into the surrounding tier-1 cluster you've been seeding. Linear stacks tend to dead-end after one promotion.

Quick drill

Spend one game forcing yourself to place every new gem on a diagonal from a same-colour gem. You'll feel the cascade difference inside three rounds.

4. Don't fight the RNG

Sometimes the queue gives you four blues in a row. Place them. Forcing a chain of greens by leaving blues in awkward spots costs more moves than just absorbing the blue run and resetting your plan. The leaderboard punishes wasted shuffles, not flexible plans.

5. End on a tier-jump, not a clear

If you can finish the round by promoting an existing tier-4 to tier-5 instead of clearing a half-merged cluster, take the promotion. Tier jumps are worth more on the primary score and don't add to your move count. Several record runs end with a single decisive promotion rather than a full-board sweep.

Putting it together

Try one pattern per session. Don't try to internalise all five at once — the cognitive load makes you play worse, not better. Most players see a 20-30% move reduction after a week of focusing on diagonals alone.

Most players see a 20-30% move reduction after a week of focusing on diagonals alone.

If you climb into the top ten this month with a strategy not on this list, send us a replay link and we'll feature it in the next post.

item.title: Welcome to the ArcadeDeck Devlog
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: We're opening a public devlog. Patch notes, behind-the-scenes posts on game design, and monthly Hall of Fame recaps will all live here.
item.content:encoded:
ArcadeDeck started as a quiet experiment: build small, original browser games with tight controls, plug them into shared leaderboards, and see what sticks. Sixteen playable titles later, the platform has grown beyond what we can comfortably announce in a single tweet. So we're starting a devlog.

Three kinds of posts will land here:

Patch notes

Every meaningful balance change, content drop, or bug fix on a published game gets a short write-up. We will explain what changed and why, and where relevant we will share the data that drove the decision (heatmaps from Galaxy Launch, win-rate splits from Spirit Duel, click-distribution charts from 15s Click Challenge). If a game gets harder or easier, we want you to understand the reasoning rather than guess.

Design deep-dives

How do you tune a roguelike's difficulty curve when every run is finite? How do you keep an idle game from collapsing into a cookie-clicker grind? These are the conversations we have internally every week — and they tend to be more interesting than "version 1.4 is live." Expect a long-form post roughly once a month, focused on one specific design problem in one specific game.

Hall of Fame recaps

At the end of every month we crown the top three players across the entire ArcadeDeck catalogue. The Hall of Fame page archives the names; this devlog will tell the stories. How did the leaders earn their points? Which games trended this month? Were there any controversies on the leaderboards? If you finished in the top ten anywhere, expect a shout-out.

Why we're doing this

Most browser game portals are content aggregators. ArcadeDeck is the opposite — every game is built in-house, and the platform reflects a particular set of opinions about what makes web games fun. Sharing those opinions in writing keeps us accountable, gives players a clearer view of where the platform is heading, and (we hope) starts conversations with developers and players who care about the same things.

Got a topic in mind?

Send a note to help@arcadedeck.net. New posts are linked from the Navbar and the home page footer; you can also bookmark arcadedeck.net/blog.

See you on the leaderboards.

item.title: Hall of Fame: March 2026 Champions
item.author: noreply@arcadedeck.net (ArcadeDeck Team)
item.description: The first ArcadeDeck monthly archive is in the books. Playerkt takes the inaugural top spot at 12 points; GG and BEN round out the podium.
item.content:encoded:
March 2026 marks the first month archived to the ArcadeDeck Hall of Fame. Three players cleared the threshold to feature on the permanent record: Playerkt at 12 points, GG at 10, and BEN at 7. Congratulations to all three.

How the points broke down

Of the 16 playable games on ArcadeDeck during March, the leader board contributed points across nine of them. The biggest single contributors to the top three were Galaxy Launch (idle, three first-place finishes), GEM MERGE (puzzle, two first-place finishes including one record-setting low move count), and Triangle Battle (multiplayer, contested across many sessions).

Playerkt's 12-point total came from a remarkable five top-three finishes spread across genres — including a top-three on the deeply technical Polygon Invasion TD, which most players bounce off in their first session. GG concentrated on action and arcade titles (Gate of Hell, 15s Click Challenge, Skyfall), and BEN posted a strong showing on the strategy side (Kingdom's Last Stand, Endless War, Spirit Duel).

Trends we noticed

March's leaderboards skewed heavily toward arcade and casual titles. The longer-form strategy and roguelike games (Dicefall Chronicles, Heroes of the Last Nexus) had top-five activity but lower volume — typical for genres where a single run can run 30-60 minutes. We expect April to swing more strategy-heavy as players who finished March pivot toward longer sessions for the second monthly cycle.

The only game with no scored entries this month was 40th Century: Void Survivor's hardcore mode, which remains the hardest single ranking on the platform. If you crack the top 10 there, expect a featured profile in the next recap.

Playerkt's 12-point total came from five top-three finishes spread across genres — including a top-three on the deeply technical Polygon Invasion TD.

Spotlight: GEM MERGE move-count record

Playerkt's GEM MERGE first-place run finished a full board with 27 fewer moves than the previous record. We pulled the replay and the route is unusual — heavy diagonal stacking with deliberate corner reservations, which lines up with several of the patterns covered in our recent strategy post. If you're chasing the GEM MERGE leaderboard in April, that replay is worth studying.

April outlook

The April cycle is live. New monthly archives are added on the first of each month, and last month's standings stay on the Hall of Fame page indefinitely. If you didn't finish in the top three in March, the cycle resets cleanly — every player starts April at zero points.

Browse the live standings on the Hall of Fame page. See you in the next archive.
